chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) who said: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to us who said: Abu Sa'id Sahl ibn Zyad al-Adamy narrated to us who said: Ja'far ibn Bashar al-Wasiti narrated to me who said: Ubaydullah ibn Abdullah al-Dahqan narrated to us, from Durost ibn Abi Mansur al-Wasiti, from Umar ibn Azineh, from Zurarah ibn A'yan, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said:

Whoever does as much good in return for a favor as has been done for him has merely repaid the debt; whoever does more is being grateful. One who is grateful is also generous. One who knows that whatever good he does, he indeed does it for himself, will no longer expect anyone to return his favors, nor will he expect any friendship in return for his friendly deeds. Do not demand anything from others in return for what you do for yourself so as to guard your own honor. Know that anyone who asks you for something from you has indeed disregarded his own honor. So do not disregard your own reputation and fulfill his request.

key_terms.شَكُورًا: Grateful; one who acknowledges and rewards good with more than is due.
key_terms.كَافَأَ: To repay or equalize; to give an equivalent return.
key_terms.يَسْتَبْطِ: To consider slow or delayed; to expect a return.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ethical distinction between repaying a favor and showing true gratitude?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Khisal* highlights the Shia ethical hierarchy of giving, distinguishing between mere reciprocity (*kafā’ah*) and true generosity (*karam*) rooted in self-awareness. Imam Ali (AS) teaches that recognizing one’s own benefit from the act of giving eliminates the need for external validation or gratitude from others, a concept deeply resonant with the Shia emphasis on *ikhlas* (sincerity). The text further advises honoring the petitioner, reflecting the social dimension of gratitude in Shia jurisprudence and ethics.
